Abstract
We study an interval ordering problem introduced by Dürr et al. [Discrete Appl. Math. 2012] which
is motivated by applications in bioinformatics. The task is to order a given set of n intervals with
the goal of minimizing a certain objective which is defined via a given cost function f which assigns
a cost to the exposed part of each interval (that is, the pieces not covered by previous intervals).
We develop a dynamic programming approach which solves the problem with O(2npoly(n)) oracle
calls to f and arithmetic operations. Moreover, our approach yields polynomial-time algorithms
for all cost functions f such that f −f(0) is subadditive or superadditive. This answers an open
question for the function f(x) = 2x. We contrast these results by proving a running time lower
bound of 2n−1 for any algorithm that solves the problem for every function f (with oracle access
only) and further proving NP-hardness for very restricted classes of functions. Thus, we significantly
narrow the gap regarding the computational complexity of the problem.

Introduction
We study the f-Interval Ordering problem introduced by Dürr et al. [4] where we are given
a set I of n intervals Ij = [aj, bj) ⊂R with aj < bj for j = 1, . . . , n and the task is to find a
total ordering of the intervals that minimizes the overall costs depending on the “exposed
parts” of the intervals. For an ordering σ = (σ(1), . . . , σ(n)) ∈Sn (where Sn denotes the set of
permutations of {1, . . . , n}), the exposed part of an interval Ij is Eσ,j := Ij\S
i:σ−1(i)<σ−1(j) Ii,
that is, the subset of Ij which is not “covered” by intervals coming before Ij in σ (see Figure 1
for an illustration). Note that Eσ,j is a union of disjoint intervals. Its length |Eσ,j| is
defined as the total sum of the lengths of its individual intervals (an interval [a, b) has
length |[a, b)| := b −a). Now, a given cost function f : [0, ∞) →R assigns a cost to each
interval depending on the length of its exposed part. Formally, the decision problem is
defined as follows.
▶Problem 1. f-Interval Ordering.
▶Input:
A set I = {I1, . . . , In} of non-empty intervals Ij = [aj, bj) ⊂R and a
number W ∈R.
▶Question: Is there an ordering σ ∈Sn such that Pn
j=1 f(|Eσ,j|) ≤W?
The f-Interval Ordering problem is motivated by a problem in biochemistry called
protein folding, that is, computing the spatial structure of a protein (a large molecule
consisting of many different atoms linked together). A simplified version of the problem is

to reconstruct the protein backbone, that is, to determine the position of the main string
of atoms (a special case of the well-studied distance geometry problem [1, 3, 6, 7, 8]). This
problem can be simplified to a certain bitstring reconstruction problem where the goal is to
find a binary string such that for given index intervals, the corresponding substring equals
an unknown string. Equality can only be tested via an oracle, which means that one has
to try all possible substrings in the worst case. In short, f-Interval Ordering with
integral intervals and f(x) = 2x corresponds to finding a process order of the intervals which
minimizes the overall number of oracle tests (see Dürr et al. [4, Section 2] for a detailed
exposition and further literature references). Besides this direct application, f-Interval
Ordering is a natural interval scheduling problem which might find further applications
and which we believe to be of independent interest on its own.
Dürr et al. [4] showed that f-Interval Ordering is NP-hard for a rather artificial
(discontinuous non-monotonic) cost function f, but solvable in polynomial time if the input
intervals are agreeable, that is, there is an ordering induced by the left interval end points
which is the same as an ordering induced by the right end points. They also prove polynomial-
time solvability for laminar intervals (that is, for every two intervals Ii, Ij, either Ii ∩Ij = ∅
or one is contained in the other) if the function f −f(0) is superadditive (note that their
NP-hardness result holds for laminar intervals). Most importantly, they posed the open
question whether the problem is polynomial-time solvable for the cost function f(x) = 2x,
which constitutes the motivating use-case in biochemistry.
Our Results.
In this work, we answer this question positively showing that f-Interval
Ordering can be solved in polynomial time for all functions f for which f −f(0) is
superadditive. Our main contribution is a dynamic programming algorithm described in
Section 3 that solves f-Interval Ordering for arbitrary cost functions in O

consider all possible exposed (and covered) parts instead of the intervals themselves. This

in O

Preliminaries
For n ∈N, we define [n] := {1, . . . , n}. A function f : [0, ∞) →R is superadditive (subadditive)
if f(x + y) ≥f(x) + f(y) (f(x + y) ≤f(x) + f(y)) for all x, y ∈[0, ∞).
We consider intervals of the form I = [a, b) ⊂R with a < b ∈R. We call a the start
point and b the end point of I. The length |I| of I is defined as b −a. We say that two
intervals Ii and Ij touch each other if they are disjoint and their union is an interval. For a set
I = {I1, . . . , In} of intervals and a permutation σ ∈Sn, we call the tuple
�Iσ(1), . . . , Iσ(n)

a
sequence of I. We say that Ii comes before Ij if σ−1(i) < σ−1(j). For a subset I′ ⊆I, we call
C(I′) := S
I∈I′ I the covered area of I′. Note that C(I′) is a union of some pairwise disjoint
intervals. We call the intervals in the smallest set of intervals whose union equals C(I′) the
interval components of C(I′) (an empty covered area has no interval components). If C(I′)
is an interval, then we call it a covered interval. We define CI := {C(I′) | I′ ⊆I}. Note
that the exposed part Eσ,j of Ij is exactly Ij \ C(I′), where I′ = {Ii | σ−1(i) < σ−1(j)}.
Again, we call the intervals of the smallest set of intervals whose union is Eσ,j, the interval
components of Eσ,j. We define EI := {Eσ,j | Ij ∈I, σ ∈Sn} \ {∅}.
Throughout this work, we assume that the cost function f : [0, ∞) →R is computable
and we neglect the time required to compute it and also the running times for arithmetic
operations.

4

Subadditive f −f(0)
First, we have a look at cost functions f where f −f(0) is subadditive, that is, f(a) +
f(b) ≥f(a + b) + f(0) holds for all a, b ∈[0, ∞) (for example, every subadditive function f
with f(0) ≤0). For such functions, we show the following.
▶Lemma 6. Let f be a cost function such that f −f(0) is subadditive. Then there is an
optimal sequence where all exposed parts are intervals.
Proof. Assume that (I1, . . . , In) is an optimal sequence where Ij has an exposed part Ej
that is not an interval, that is, it has at least two interval components. This means that the
covered area of {I1, . . . , Ij−1} has an interval component that is a subinterval of Ij. Therefore,
the intervals before Ij that cover this interval component are also subintervals of Ij (see
Figure 3). Let those intervals be Ii1, . . . , Iik and let their exposed parts be Ei1, . . . , Eik. Now
consider what happens if we change Ii1, . . . , Iik to come after Ij. Then the exposed parts
of Ii1, . . . , Iik will be empty and the exposed part of Ij will increase by |Ei1| + · · · + |Eik|.
Subadditivity now yields
f(|Ei1|) + · · · + f(|Eik|) + f(|Ej|) ≥f(|Ei1| + · · · + |Eik| + |Ej|) + k · f(0),
that is, the cost does not increase. This rearrangement reduces the number of interval
components of the exposed part of Ij while not increasing the number of interval components
of any other exposed part. Therefore, after a finite number of rearrangements we obtain an
optimal sequence where all exposed parts are intervals.

4.2
Superadditive f −f(0)
If f −f(0) is superadditive, then f(a + b) + f(0) ≥f(a) + f(b) holds for all a, b ∈[0, ∞) (for
example, every superadditive function with f(0) ≥0). This case is of special interest because
such cost functions are somewhat natural for applications (like the function 2x in the original
motivation). Again, we observe a special structure of optimal sequences for this case.
▶Lemma 10. Let f be a cost function such that f −f(0) is superadditive. Then there is an
optimal sequence where no interval comes before any of its proper subintervals.
Proof. Assume that there is an optimal sequence where an interval Ii comes after the
interval Ij, but Ii is a proper subset of Ij. Let Ei = ∅and Ej be the exposed parts of Ii
and Ij respectively. Consider what happens when we change the interval Ii to be right before
the interval Ij. Then, only the exposed parts of Ii and Ij can change. The exposed part of Ii
will be Ej ∩Ii and the exposed part of Ij will be Ej \ Ii (see Figure 4). By superadditivity,
it holds:
f(|Ei|) + f(|Ej|) = f(0) + f(|Ej ∩Ii| + |Ej \ Ii|) ≥f(|Ej ∩Ii|) + f(|Ej \ Ii|).
Therefore, the cost does not increase. We can repeat this step finitely many times until there
are no more intervals before any of their proper subintervals. As we started with an optimal
sequence and we did not increase the cost, this will be an optimal sequence as well.

5
Hardness Results
In this section, we complement our algorithmic results from the previous sections with
running time lower bounds and NP-hardness.
5.1
Exponential Running Time Lower Bound
We show that the exponential part of O(2n) in the running time of Algorithm 1 from
Section 3 is basically optimal. More precisely, we prove that every deterministic algorithm
that computes an optimal interval ordering for every f without knowledge about f (that is,
it is only provided an oracle for f which outputs f(x) in constant time) takes at least 2n−1
time (in the worst case). To prove this lower bound, we show that f must be evaluated at
all distinct lengths of exposed parts, of which there can be exponentially many.
▶Lemma 14. For all n ≥2, there exists a set I of n intervals with |{|E| | E ∈EI}| ≥2n−1
such that, for each E ∈EI, there is an ordering of I where no interval has an exposed part
of length |E|.

In this section, we introduce a more fine-grained analysis of the computational complexity
of f-Interval Ordering. To this end, we identify certain parameters which render the
problem tractable when their values are small (constants). As the exponential part of the

Our first parameter is the maximum number of interval components of any exposed part

7
Conclusion
We took a large step towards settling the computational complexity of the interval ordering
problem. As regards the cost function, we showed broad families of functions to be polynomial-
time solvable while we showed NP-hardness already for some very restricted functions. It
might be interesting to further close the gap between the tractable and intractable cases
by identifying the specific properties that render a function tractable. For example, the
complexity for subadditive and superadditive functions is open.
Regarding running times, on one side, there is clearly the challenge to improve the
polynomial running times. This may allow experiments on real-world datasets in order to
evaluate whether integrating an f-Interval Ordering solver into actual protein backbone
reconstruction algorithms is worth the computation overhead. On the other side, proving

conditional running time lower bounds for the polynomial-time solvable cases would also
be interesting. Moreover, we initiated the study of the parameterized complexity of the
problem. It could be fruitful to identify parameters which render instances tractable in
practice. For example, it is open whether the problem is fixed-parameter tractable for the
maximum number αI of interval components of any exposed part.

Abstract: We study an interval ordering problem introduced by Dürr et al. [Discrete Appl. Math. 2012] which is motivated by applications in bioinformatics. The task is to order a given set of n intervals with the goal of minimizing a certain objective which is defined via a given cost function f which assigns a cost to the exposed part of each interval (that is, the pieces not covered by previous intervals). We develop a dynamic programming approach which solves the problem with O(2npoly(n)) oracle calls to f and arithmetic operations. Moreover, our approach yields polynomial-time algorithms for all cost functions f such that f −f(0) is subadditive or superadditive. This answers an open question for the function f(x) = 2x. We contrast these results by proving a running time lower bound of 2n−1 for any algorithm that solves the problem for every function f (with oracle access only) and further proving NP-hardness for very restricted classes of functions. Thus, we significantly narrow the gap regarding the computational complexity of the problem. 2012 ACM Subject Classification Theory of computation →Dynamic programming; Theory of computation →Fixed parameter tractability; Theory of computation →Problems, reductions and completeness; Applied computing →Bioinformatics
